questions.question: Which measure is the arithmetic average?
questions.explanation: Mean is the sum divided by the count.

questions.question: What is the median of 3, 7, 1, 9, 5?
questions.explanation: Sorted: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; the middle value is 5.

questions.question: What is the mode of 2, 4, 4, 6, 7?
questions.explanation: 4 appears most often (twice).

questions.question: What is the range of 4, 10, 7, 2?
questions.explanation: Range = maximum - minimum = 10 - 2 = 8.

questions.question: What is the probability of rolling an even number on a fair six-sided die?
questions.explanation: Three of the six equally likely faces (2, 4, 6) are even.

questions.question: How does a sample relate to a population?
options: A sample is a subset of the population
A sample includes the whole population
A population is a subset of a sample
They are always the same size
questions.explanation: Samples are drawn from a population to make inferences about it.

questions.question: Which of these is a categorical variable?
questions.explanation: Blood type takes category labels; the others are numeric measurements.

questions.question: What are the mean and standard deviation of the standard normal distribution?
questions.explanation: The standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) has mean 0 and variance 1.

questions.question: What does standard deviation measure?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures dispersion around the mean.

questions.question: What is the possible range of Pearson's correlation coefficient r?
questions.explanation: r is bounded between -1 (perfect negative) and +1 (perfect positive).

questions.question: What is a p-value?
options: The probability, assuming H0 is true, of results at least as extreme as those observed
The probability that H0 is true
The probability that H1 is true
The significance level chosen before the test
questions.explanation: A p-value is computed under the null hypothesis; it is not the probability that H0 is true.

questions.question: What is a Type I error?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true
questions.explanation: Type I is a false positive; its probability is the significance level alpha.

questions.question: What is the population variance of 2, 4, 6?
questions.explanation: Mean is 4; squared deviations 4, 0, 4 sum to 8; divided by N = 3 gives 8/3 (the sample variance would be 4).

questions.question: In a right-skewed (positively skewed) distribution, how do the mean and median typically compare?
questions.explanation: The long right tail pulls the mean upward more than the median.

questions.question: What is the correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval?
options: If sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter
There is a 95% chance the sample mean lies in the interval
95% of the data values lie in the interval
The parameter changes 95% of the time
questions.explanation: The 95% refers to the long-run success rate of the interval procedure.

questions.question: In a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule gives about 68%, 95% and 99.7% within 1, 2 and 3 SDs.

questions.question: What does the Central Limit Theorem state?
options: Large samples always have smaller means
The sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches normal as n grows, for populations with finite variance
The sample median equals the population mean
questions.explanation: This holds regardless of the population's shape, provided variance is finite.

questions.question: A population has standard deviation 20. What is the standard error of the mean for samples of size 100?
questions.explanation: SE = sigma / sqrt(n) = 20 / 10 = 2.

questions.question: Holding alpha and effect size fixed, what happens to a test's power when the sample size increases?
questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce standard error, making true effects easier to detect.

questions.question: What is the chi-square test of independence used for?
options: Comparing the means of two numeric groups
Testing whether two categorical variables are associated
Testing whether a variable is normally distributed
questions.explanation: It compares observed and expected counts in a contingency table.

questions.question: If A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5, what is P(A and B)?
questions.explanation: For independent events P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B) = 0.15.

questions.question: A disease has 1% prevalence. A test has 90% sensitivity and a 9% false-positive rate. Approximately what is P(disease | positive)?
